newsitem.title: BELGIUM: One-month jail term asked for Belgian paratroopers.
newsitem.headline: One-month jail term asked for Belgian paratroopers.

text.p: A Brussels military court prosecutor on Monday recommended one month's prison each for two Belgian paratroopers accused of maltreating a Somali youth during a humanitarian mission in the African country in 1993.

The two men, Kurt Coelus and Claude Baert, were identified from a photograph published in the Belgian daily Het Laatste Nieuws earlier this year which appeared to show them swinging a Somali boy over a camp fire.
Other pictures printed by the newspaper showed a soldier urinating on the apparently dead body of a Somali and one with his army boot pressed on the head of another Somali.

Coelus and Baert were in court on Monday together with their sergeant Dirk Nassel, all charged with threatening behaviour and physical violence committed while they served in the multinational peacekeeping mission in Somalia.
The first charge carries a possible sentence of between eight days and three months in prison, and the second of one month to one year behind bars.
A verdict on the Coelus-Baert case is due on June 30.
Nassel, whose case was delayed at the request of his defence, is alleged to have made a Somali Moslem boy eat pork and drink salt water.
Defence lawyers for Coelus and Baert, who deny the charges against them, said the two were merely playing games. The men also rejected accusations of racism.
The Belgian Centre for Equal Opportunities and the Fight Against Racism is acting as a civil party in the court martial and has asked for the men to be fined 100,000 Belgian francs ($2,800).

Luc Walleyn, the Centre's lawyer, said after Monday's hearing he regretted that the paratroopers' treatment of Somalis had been broken down into individual cases of physical injury "when we're confronted with something much more serious."
This, he said, was "the development - tolerated by some in charge in the army - of a racist mentality in the corps which have served under the U.N. flag in Africa."
Het Laatste Nieuws, which broke the story on March 29, on Monday quoted the men as saying they had wanted to teach the Somalis a lesson.
The newspaper was outraged. "In spite of all the indignation, even ministerial, they risk only light sentences," it said.
After Het Laatste Nieuws published the photographs of what it described as atrocities, Belgian Defence Minister Jean-Pol Poncelet described the acts as horrible and tasteless.
The allegations sparked a review of paratroop training and caused Poncelet to wonder in public whether the Third Paratroop Battalion to which the men belonged should be disbanded.

Around 1,000 Belgian troops took part in United Nations Operation Restore Hope in Somalia and even when they were still on the ground there were allegations they had massively understated the number of Somalis they had killed during military operations.
In October 1995, nine Belgian soldiers accused of maltreating Somali children were acquitted by a Brussels military court, and another was given an eight-day suspended jail sentence.
The charges against the three on trial on Monday mirrored those made separately against members of Canadian and Italian forces who also served for the United Nations in Somalia.

Italian President Oscar Luigi Scalfaro said on Saturday that Italy would try to shed light quickly on allegations that Rome's troops, who served in Somalia from late 1992 to early 1994, had engaged in torture and rape there.
Italian army generals said many of the allegations were false or exaggerated. ($ = 35.66 Belgian Francs)
